anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions request mutually incompatible locks on the same objects, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall transaction progress.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database components collectively consume more physical memory than the host can safely supply, leading to paging, OOM events, and cache-churn side effects.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate available CPU cores so that runnable tasks pile up and every operation experiences scheduler delay.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers heavy lock waits, runaway memory growth, and CPU saturation. Each symptom originates in its own layer but co-exists in the same runtime window, producing an OLTP environment where sessions are both blocked on locks and starved for memory and CPU, making the overall system appear hung or intermittently unresponsive.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Lock-wait and deadlock diagnostics show long blocker–waiter chains, yet even unblocked requests execute slowly because CPU run queues are full and memory paging stalls I/O. 2) Process RSS and OS swap metrics rise while lock tables stop shrinking because victim rollbacks themselves need memory and CPU to complete. 3) Application timeouts, connection-pool exhaustion, and surge in retry storms coincide with host load averages pegged near core count and kernel swapping spikes, creating erratic throughput and latency outliers.

Causal chain and mutual reinforcement: Excessive memory allocation inflates the working set, provoking the OS to swap; paging overhead steals CPU cycles and pushes the run queue higher. CPU starvation lengthens every critical section, so transactions hold locks longer, deepening contention and increasing the probability of deadlocks. Conversely, lock blockage forces sessions to stay active, retaining their work buffers and execution state, which amplifies memory pressure. When victims are rolled back, they often re-execute, adding even more CPU demand and memory churn. The three anomalies therefore form a feedback loop—memory pressure and CPU saturation slow lock release, extended locking enlarges session memory footprints, and the retransmission of aborted work keeps CPU utilization maxed—driving the database into a progressively worsening spiral until intervention or load shedding occurs.

entry.official_description: Still rolling back transaction %llu; %llu undo records rolled back out of %llu total (%lu%% complete). Transaction info: last state: %s
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
